The paper was published in 1992 by Tom Cwik at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Caltech.
Parallel supercomputers consist of interconnected microprocessors, often hundreds to thousands, achieving performance rivaling or surpassing conventional supercomputers.
Flynn's taxonomy classifies computer architectures into SISD, SIMD, MIMD, and MISD; MIMD is most relevant for current parallel machines.
Shared-memory machines have fewer processors (1-64) with large shared memory; distributed-memory machines have many processors each with local memory.
Distributed-memory machines can have hypercube or mesh topologies for processor interconnection.
Coarse-grained distributed-memory machines typically operate in MIMD mode with 8 to 4000 processors and 4 to 64 MB memory per processor.
Fine-grained machines operate in SIMD mode with thousands to over 100,000 simple processors and small memory per processor.
Problem decomposition divides the computational domain into grains, each mapped to a processor with associated memory.
Load imbalance occurs when grain sizes vary, reducing parallel efficiency due to some processors idling.
FDTD uses a regular Cartesian grid allowing straightforward block decomposition with minimal communication limited to block boundaries.
Field updates in FDTD comprise over 90% of computation time; communication overhead is small due to volume-to-surface scaling.
Radiation condition enforcement and radar cross section (RCS) calculations in FDTD are less load-balanced and reduce efficiency slightly.
Finite element method uses unstructured mesh leading to irregular problem domains and sparse matrices with less straightforward decomposition.
Sparse matrices in FEM have very few nonzero entries per row (<100) but can be very large (rank >100,000).
Parallel FEM decomposition involves dividing mesh data, computing sparse matrix entries locally, solving the sparse system, and calculating RCS.
Loosely synchronous parallel computations require processors to synchronize periodically for data exchange.
Fixed-grain scaling allows solving larger problems as processors increase, maintaining constant data per processor.
Fixed-size scaling solves the same problem on more processors, reducing time but increasing communication overhead.
Communication overhead limits scalability, leading to diminishing returns beyond a certain number of processors.
The paper suggests that future system software may assist in automatic problem decomposition, but currently, user intervention is needed.
